title: Zacharias Frankel
hookLine: a rabbi walks out of a meeting and starts looking for a middle path between tradition and history

lines: A ROOM OF RABBIS IN FRANKFURT.
cards: A room full of rabbis in Frankfurt, deep in a long argument. The question sounds small: does Jewish prayer have to be in Hebrew? The meeting leans toward an answer: Hebrew is welcome, but not required.

One rabbi, Zacharias Frankel, listens, gathers his papers and leaves. He doesn't cross over to the other camp either. He spends the rest of his life looking for a road between the two camps in that room.

teach.b: By Frankel's day, German Jews were splitting into camps. The reformers, two days ago, wanted to change prayer and practice to fit modern life.
Hirsch, yesterday, held that the law was given whole, to be lived fully inside the modern world.
Frankel agreed fully with neither. He was a scholar of history. He read the Mishnah and the Talmud the way a historian reads, asking when a law took shape, and how, and why.
He was ready to say that Jewish law had grown and changed over time. That sounded like the reformers. But he drew a different conclusion.
If the law grew inside the life of the people, then the people's long practice carries real weight. Hebrew in prayer was not a habit to drop. It was part of the living body of Judaism.
So change could come, but slowly, from inside, with respect for what the people had actually kept.
His name for this was positive-historical Judaism. Positive, because the tradition is given and real. Historical, because it has a history and is still moving.
He went on to lead a new rabbinical seminary in Breslau, where students learned both the texts and the methods of history. Conservative Judaism, which grew later, looks back on him as a forerunner.
Jeremiah has a line that fits his instinct.

The prophet tells the people to stand in the ways and look, and to "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein." Not frozen where the roads meet, and not running off in a new direction.
Ask the old paths, then walk.

how: Conservative Jewish communities study Jewish law alongside its history, and their rabbis make rulings on change through committees that weigh both the tradition and the practice of the community.

games.q: you are Frankel at the meeting. the room leans toward saying Hebrew in prayer is welcome but not required. what do you do?
games.why: he left, and spent the rest of his life working out a middle path between reform and strict tradition.

practice: Bring to mind one old habit, yours or your family's, that someone would like to change. Before deciding anything, ask what it has carried all these years. Then let one small change appear that keeps what it carried and still moves.

wordCard.voice: Zacharias Frankel. The German rabbi and historian who walked out of a debate over Hebrew prayer and taught that Jewish law is both given and growing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle path. Change can come, slowly and from inside. Until next time.
